No command substitutions (e.g., $(curl ...), `curl ...`, or other dynamic code execution) occur in the global scope. The functions `pkgver()`, `build()`, and `package()` are defined but will not be executed during `makepkg --printsrcinfo`, so they are out of scope for this narrow gate. There is no evidence of malicious code execution, data exfiltration, or unauthorized network activity triggered simply by sourcing the PKGBUILD.

The provided `.SRCINFO` file is a metadata file commonly found in Arch User Repository (AUR) packages. No executable code or suspicious commands are present in this file. The dependencies and architecture declarations are appropriate for a GTK-based image viewer with support for modern image formats.

There is no evidence of obfuscated commands, unauthorized network activity, or malicious payloads. The file does not execute any code or modify system settings outside of standard packaging practices. It solely serves as metadata for building the package via `makepkg`, which is consistent with AUR conventions. The `conflicts` and `provides` fields are correctly used to manage package naming collisions, indicating responsible packaging.

This file does not introduce any supply-chain risks on its own. While it references a mutable git source (common for `-git` packages), that is expected behavior and not a security flaw by itself.

The `pkgver()` function uses `git describe` to generate a version string based on the latest tag and commit, a common pattern in `-git` packages.

The build process uses `cmake` to compile the code from the checked-out source directory, which is standard for CMake-based projects. The `package()` function installs built files into `$pkgdir`, along with documentation and license files, using standard `install` commands. All operations are confined to the build directory and package destination, with no unexpected system modifications or network activity.

There are no signs of obfuscated code, unauthorized downloads, or execution of external scripts. The dependencies are appropriate for an image viewer with rich format support, and the use of `cmake --install` aligns with modern build practices. While the source tracks a mutable git reference (normal for `-git` packages), there is no `git pull` during build, so the risk of unchecked updates is absent.
</details>
